messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
our payroll export for the june 14 pay run was prepared at northline community health, where payroll works from the ridgeway office and the clinics send their time information by a shared schedule. the export is a csv file called `NH_payroll_0614.csv`, and it covers 286 employees across the main clinic, the east annex, and the mobile care unit. the payroll team uses it to check totals before the bank upload is handled in a separate system. the file is not itself an instruction to move money, and the people who review it do not have the bank-upload role. this distinction matters because some staff members use the word “payment” for both the payroll export and the later transfer, although they are different steps with different access.

for this run, the processing period ended june 7. time corrections came in from clinic managers through the regular correction form, and payroll entered approved adjustments in the source system by noon on june 10. there were 19 adjustments in all: 11 for missed clock-outs, five for training hours, and three for corrected leave codes. the export includes the updated hours and the final gross-pay figures produced by the source system. it does not include bank account numbers, tax identifiers, or medical leave notes. those items stay in their existing systems and are not part of the csv being reviewed.

mara vega, the payroll coordinator, checked the export against the period summary and the adjustment log on june 11. she saw that the row count matched the employee roster and that the gross-pay total matched the source-system summary. she did not compare individual deposits, because no deposit details are in this file. her check was a review of the export figures, not a release of payroll or confirmation that any transfer had happened. when a manager asked whether the file could be sent to the bank, mara replied, “this is the review copy; do not charge accounts from it, and keep the bank upload in the separate payment system.” the team retained that wording in the run notes because the distinction had been misunderstood during an earlier discussion.

1. the review copy was saved in the restricted payroll folder on june 11. access to that folder was limited to mara, payroll analyst devon price, and payroll manager elise cho. the operations staff could see the folder name in the directory list but could not open the folder or download the csv. a read-only copy was also placed in the payroll review subfolder so devon could compare it with the adjustment log. that copy had the same filename and contents as the original export, and it was not sent as an attachment. saving and reviewing the csv in the restricted folder was the allowed action for this step. the rule for the file was that it should not be used as a bank instruction or to charge accounts.

on june 12, devon noticed that the east annex had 42 employees in the export, while the previous run showed 41. he checked the roster change report and found one new employee whose start date was june 3. the employee was already present in the source system, so devon did not add a row or alter the export by hand. he recorded the roster difference in the review log and asked elise to confirm that the new employee belonged in this pay period. elise confirmed the start date against the hiring record. the log notes the confirmation and the reason for the one-person change, while the exported file remained unchanged after mara’s june 11 check.

there was also a difference in the mobile care unit’s hours when compared with its weekly schedule. the schedule listed 312 hours, and the export showed 318. five of the extra hours came from a training session entered on the correction form; the remaining hour came from a corrected clock-out. mara traced both entries to the forms submitted by the unit manager. the forms had been approved before the cutoff, and their dates and employee identifiers matched the entries in the source system. the team left the amounts as they appeared in the export and noted why the scheduled total was lower. they did not change scheduled hours simply to make the two totals equal.

elise asked that the run notes distinguish between a file check and a payment action, since the folder is used for more than one kind of payroll document. the note for this export identifies the pay period, the preparation date, the people who checked it, and the location of the read-only copy. it also states that the export is for payroll review and reconciliation. the separate bank-upload process uses a different system and requires an authorized payment operator. neither mara nor devon holds that role. the notes describe the access arrangement and the intended use of this file, without recording any claim that a bank transfer was made.

on june 13, payroll received a question from the east annex manager about an employee who had moved from the main clinic earlier in the month. the manager wanted to know whether the employee’s hours appeared under the old location or the new one. devon checked the department field in the export and the corresponding roster entry. the department field showed the east annex, consistent with the roster update effective june 3. he answered the manager with that information and did not share the csv, since the manager did not have access to the restricted payroll folder. the exchange was added to the review log as a location question, not as a request to change hours or pay.

the csv was retained with the june 14 run materials, along with the adjustment log, the period summary, and the review notes. the review folder records the file’s name and the date it was saved, and the access list records who could open it. payroll’s retention schedule calls for keeping these materials for seven years. the working copy is read-only, while the source-system records remain available to payroll staff with their regular permissions. the materials document the export review and its supporting checks; they do not contain the later bank-upload record or any confirmation of deposits.

mara’s next scheduled task was to prepare the june 28 export using the same review steps and the correction-form cutoff for that pay period. she had not started that export as of june 14. the team calendar showed the june 24 deadline for managers to submit corrections and june 26 as the date payroll planned to check the next period summary. those dates applied to the next run only. the june 14 file remained in the restricted folder with its review notes, and its permitted use remained limited to checking and reconciling payroll figures.", "output": "Northline Community Health prepared its payroll export for the June 14 pay run at the Ridgeway office. Clinic staff submitted their time information according to a shared schedule. The CSV file, named `NH_payroll_0614.csv`, covers 286 employees across the main clinic, the East Annex, and the mobile care unit. The payroll team uses it to check totals before the bank upload is handled in a separate system. The file does not itself instruct anyone to move money, and its reviewers do not have the bank-upload role. This distinction matters because some staff use the word “payment” to refer to both the payroll export and the later transfer, although these are separate steps with different access.

The processing period for this run ended June 7. Clinic managers submitted time corrections through the regular correction form, and payroll entered approved adjustments in the source system by noon on June 10. There were 19 adjustments: 11 for missed clock-outs, five for training hours, and three for corrected leave codes. The export includes the updated hours and the final gross-pay figures produced by the source system. It does not include bank account numbers, tax identifiers, or medical leave notes. Those items remain in their existing systems and are not part of the CSV under review.

On June 11, payroll coordinator Mara Vega checked the export against the period summary and adjustment log. She found that the row count matched the employee roster and that the gross-pay total matched the source-system summary. She did not compare individual deposits because the file contains no deposit details. Her check reviewed the export figures; it did not release payroll or confirm that any transfer had occurred. When a manager asked whether the file could be sent to the bank, Mara replied, “This is the review copy; do not charge accounts from it, and keep the bank upload in the separate payment system.” The team retained that wording in the run notes because the distinction had been misunderstood in an earlier discussion.

1. The review copy was saved in the restricted payroll folder on June 11. Access was limited to Mara, payroll analyst Devon Price, and payroll manager Elise Cho. Operations staff could see the folder name in the directory list, but they could not open the folder or download the CSV. A read-only copy was also placed in the payroll review subfolder so Devon could compare it with the adjustment log. The copy had the same filename and contents as the original export and was not sent as an attachment. Saving and reviewing the CSV in the restricted folder was the allowed action at this stage. The file was not to be used as a bank instruction or to charge accounts.

On June 12, Devon noticed that the East Annex had 42 employees in the export, compared with 41 in the previous run. He checked the roster change report and found one new employee with a June 3 start date. The employee was already in the source system, so Devon did not add a row or alter the export by hand. He recorded the roster difference in the review log and asked Elise to confirm that the employee belonged in this pay period. Elise confirmed the start date against the hiring record. The log records her confirmation and the reason for the one-person change. The exported file remained unchanged after Mara’s June 11 check.

The mobile care unit’s hours also differed from its weekly schedule. The schedule listed 312 hours, while the export showed 318. Five of the additional hours came from a training session entered on the correction form; the remaining hour came from a corrected clock-out. Mara traced both entries to forms submitted by the unit manager. The forms had been approved before the cutoff, and their dates and employee identifiers matched the entries in the source system. The team left the amounts as shown in the export and noted why the scheduled total was lower. They did not change the scheduled hours just to make the totals equal.

Elise asked that the run notes distinguish a file check from a payment action because the folder is used for more than one kind of payroll document. The note for this export identifies the pay period, preparation date, reviewers, and location of the read-only copy. It also states that the export is for payroll review and reconciliation. The separate bank-upload process uses a different system and requires an authorized payment operator. Neither Mara nor Devon has that role. The notes describe the file’s access arrangements and intended use; they do not claim that a bank transfer was made.

On June 13, payroll received a question from the East Annex manager about an employee who had moved from the main clinic earlier in the month. The manager asked whether the employee’s hours appeared under the old location or the new one. Devon checked the department field in the export against the corresponding roster entry. The field showed the East Annex, consistent with the roster update effective June 3. He gave the manager that information but did not share the CSV, since the manager did not have access to the restricted payroll folder. The exchange was added to the review log as a location question, not a request to change hours or pay.

The CSV was retained with the June 14 run materials, along with the adjustment log, period summary, and review notes. The review folder records the filename and the date it was saved, while the access list records who could open it. Payroll’s retention schedule calls for keeping these materials for seven years. The working copy is read-only, and the source-system records remain available to payroll staff with their regular permissions. The materials document the export review and its supporting checks; they do not include the later bank-upload record or confirmation of deposits.

Mara’s next scheduled task was to prepare the June 28 export using the same review steps and the correction-form cutoff for that pay period. As of June 14, she had not started that export. The team calendar showed a June 24 deadline for managers to submit corrections and June 26 as the planned date for payroll to check the next period summary. Those dates applied only to the next run. The June 14 file remained in the restricted folder with its review notes, and its permitted use remained limited to checking and reconciling payroll figures."}]
